data.name: Kalil
data.gender_notes: Kalil is used as a male name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: In Arabic, Kalil is derived from the root K-L-L, which means 'to be wise' or 'to be clever'. In Islamic tradition, it is believed that the name Kalil was given to the legendary king of Babel, who was known for his wisdom and knowledge. The name Kalil carries the meaning “Wise, Clever” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Kalil usually hope their child will grow to embody wise, clever and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: A symbol of wisdom and knowledge.
data.etymology: Kalil belongs to the Arabic linguistic tradition and is used in Islamic naming. Its recorded meaning is “Wise, Clever.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Kalil total 9, giving a life-path number of 9. Number 9 is linked with Mars and with the qualities of compassion, idealism and generosity.

data.cultural_impact: The name Kalil has a rich cultural significance in Islamic tradition, as it is linked to the story of King Kalilah and Dimna, which is a part of One Thousand and One Nights or The Arabian Nights. The story is about the cleverness and wisdom of King Kalilah, who ruled over Babylon before the time of Prophet Sheeth. Through various anecdotes and tales, he used his wisdom to rule his people justly and to teach them valuable moral lessons. This literary legacy has not only formed an integral part of Islamic folklore but has also contributed significantly to the world's literary heritage.
data.spiritual_significance: The spiritual significance of the name Kalil lies in the fact that it symbolizes wisdom and knowledge from the divine perspective. In the Islamic context, gaining the knowledge of Allah SWT and applying it in one's daily life is highly regarded. The name serves as a constant reminder to seek knowledge and wisdom, not only for personal growth but also to help others and spread peace and understanding in the world. It inspires one to be resourceful, ingenious, and creative, just like King Kalilah, in order to create a harmonious and just society.

historical_references.reference: Ibn Al-Nafis's work 'Theologus Autodidactus', 13th century CE, contained a philosophical discussion about the nature of God and included a parable known as 'The Story of Kalila and Dimna'. This parable is a collection of animal fables, similar to Aesop's fables.

historical_references.reference: The 'One Thousand and One Nights' or 'Arabian Nights', a collection of Middle Eastern folktales and legends, was first compiled in Arabic during the Islamic Golden Age in the 14th century CE. 'The Story of Kalila and Dimna' is one of the most famous stories within this collection and has been retold in various forms throughout history, including in Europe during the Renaissance.
